# TrajLift: Lifting Memory Recall Trajectories with Latency-Modulated Heat Diffusion
###### Abstract
Our central mechanism is latency-modulated heat diffusion on the semantic hierarchy, a unified operator that lifts each recalled word into a representation of both multi-scale hierarchical structure and continuous retrieval timing. Formal analysis shows that the resulting representation is first-order separable into structural and temporal components with spectral selectivity across hierarchical levels. On synthetic benchmarks requiring structure-time interaction, TrajLift stays near-perfect on deep hierarchies where all baselines fail.
## 1 Introduction
In this work, we model verbal retrieval as a graph heat diffusion process on the semantic hierarchy, where each recalled word is treated as a localized signal on the graph that spreads to its structural neighborhood. Heat diffusion on hierarchically weighted graphs has the well-known property that the diffusion time (i.e., a continuous scalar) controls the structural resolution of the resulting representation. We exploit this to lift each node visit to progressively coarser hierarchical scales, capturing within-category and cross-domain structure.
We further extend this framework to encode temporal dynamics by letting the observed inter-item latency modulate the diffusion time within a bounded range, so that latency alters the representation at each scale without changing which hierarchical level that scale resolves. Formal analysis shows that under this formulation, the structural and temporal signals are first-order separable, and that the temporal encoding is sensitive to the hierarchical level.

# A Neural Chronometry of Memory Recall
## Abstract
Electrophysiological recordings suggest that sensory cues proceed into the medial temporal lobe within the first 500 ms. At this point, a hippocampal process sets in, geared toward internal pattern completion and coordination of cortical memory reinstatement between 500 and 1500 ms. We further highlight the dynamic principles governing the recall process, which include a reversal of perceptual information flows, temporal compression, and theta clocking.
## The Temporal Codes of Memory Recall
As reviewed above, accumulating evidence suggests that hippocampal–neocortical dynamics between 500 and 1500 ms after a reminder reinstate mnemonic patterns. In this section, we zoom in on the temporal dynamics that govern the reinstatement process in this critical time window. We first review the evidence regarding the timeline of memory reactivation for single events and event sequences, before turning to the role of theta oscillations in clocking the reinstatement process.
### Theta Oscillations as a Clocking Mechanism
As expected, decoding of reactivated mnemonic content was maximal 500–1000 ms after cue onset, consistent with the literature reviewed above. Critically, in this time window the neural signatures of memory reinstatement fluctuated rhythmically, waxing and waning at a theta frequency of 8 Hz (Figure 3 B, bottom left).
Together, electrophysiological recordings support the idea that content reinstatement during memory recall follows reminder-specific processing with a latency of ∼200 ms, roughly corresponding to one theta cycle. Some temporal variability is, of course, to be expected empirically and it is unlikely that perceptual versus mnemonic processes occur in an all-or-none fashion at a single instance of a theta cycle.

A key challenge is that timing and hierarchical structure are diagnostically entangled: the diagnostic meaning of retrieval timing depends on its hierarchical context. We propose TrajLift, a spectral framework that models verbal recall as timed trajectories on a hierarchical graph. Verbal memory assessments, such as the California Verbal Learning Test (CVLT) [2] and Hong Kong List Learning Test (HKLLT) [15], evaluate cognitive decline by requiring subjects to recall word lists across multiple trials. Recent work has moved beyond total scores to process-level measures of recall [16], however, such measures, like text-based encoders, reduce a recall sequence to aggregate statistics or a flat string. They overlook the fundamental nature of verbal retrieval as the navigation of a structured cognitive map [5], in which the sequence of recalled items forms a specific path through semantic space. To the best of our knowledge, graph-theoretic modeling of this retrieval path remains underexplored.

### 2.2 Inductive Biases in Graph Trajectory Learning

Modeling retrieval paths requires aligning inductive biases with the cognitive process: a continuous signal evolving over a static hierarchy. Existing paradigms, however, often misalign with this specific setting. First, regarding dynamics, Continuous-Time Dynamic Graph (CTDG) models [17, 18], such as TGN [9] and TGAT [10], predominantly focus on dynamics of graphs (evolving topology). This edge-centric bias is suboptimal for our scenario, where the semantic substrate is invariant and the diagnostic signal lies solely in the trajectory of node activations. Second, regarding trajectory and hierarchy, while spatial models like TrajGAT [12] and TrajDiff [19] capture sequential patterns, and encoders like Graphormers [20, 21] or R-GCNs [22] handle global structure, they typically process transitions as discrete steps. Consequently, these architectures lack a mechanism to model continuous inter-item latencies in relation to the structure in which they occur. They therefore cannot capture how the meaning of a latency (e.g., hesitation) depends on its position in the semantic hierarchy.

## Abstract

Verbal memory retrieval carries rich diagnostic information for Alzheimer's disease through the order, hesitation, and categorical organization of recalled words, yet computational modeling of this retrieval process remains largely unexplored. A key challenge is that timing and hierarchical structure are diagnostically entangled: the diagnostic meaning of retrieval timing depends on its hierarchical context. We propose TrajLift, a spectral framework that models verbal recall as timed trajectories on a hierarchical graph. Our central mechanism is latency-modulated heat diffusion on the semantic hierarchy, a unified operator that lifts each recalled word into a representation of both multi-scale hierarchical structure and continuous retrieval timing. Formal analysis shows that the resulting representation is first-order separable into structural and temporal components with spectral selectivity across hierarchical levels. On synthetic benchmarks requiring structure-time interaction, TrajLift stays near-perfect on deep hierarchies where all baselines fail. On real-world clinical data, we show that TrajLift outperforms diverse baselines by jointly modeling timing and semantic structure, with gains that grow as retrieval timing becomes more informative.

**2026-11-16****Fast at the Frontier, Wrong at the Fallback: A Commit-Level Analysis of Threshold Decoding in Diffusion Language Models**cs.CL, cs.LG Full Abstract Diffusion language models (DLMs) can write several tokens per forward pass. Open-weight DLMs commit, in any order, every masked position whose confidence passes a threshold. If none does, a fallback commits the most confident one, and the commits are never revised. Wide windows let the decoder commit far ahead of the text, which should speed up decoding but often costs accuracy. It is unclear where the model is confident and which commits cause errors. We trace every commit of four off-the-shelf DLMs on math, code, translation and summarization, and rerun failing answers with one step changed. Most tokens become confident only near the frontier, the leftmost masked position, so committing only there, still several tokens per step, is about as fast as committing anywhere. The accuracy loss comes from committing tokens before the text to their left, and committing one token per step does not reduce it. The worst case is an early end-of-sequence token that cuts the answer short. Fallback commits are 11-35% of commits but start 61-72% of the failures that left-to-right decoding avoids. Changing only the step where such a failure starts repairs it more often than changing a similar earlier step. Committing only at the frontier recovers most of the lost accuracy on all four models. In this work, we model verbal retrieval as a graph heat diffusion process on the semantic hierarchy,
where each recalled word is treated as a localized signal on the graph that spreads to its structural
neighborhood. Heat diffusion on hierarchically weighted graphs has the well-known property that the
diffusion time (i.e., a continuous scalar) controls the structural resolution of the resulting represen-
tation. We exploit this to lift each node visit to progressively coarser hierarchical scales, capturing
within-category and cross-domain structure. We further extend this framework to encode temporal
dynamics by letting the observed inter-item latency modulate the diffusion time within a bounded
range, so that latency alters the representation at each scale without changing which hierarchical level
that scale resolves. Formal analysis shows that under this formulation, the structural and temporal
signals are first-order separable, and that the temporal encoding is sensitive to the hierarchical level.

Spectral lifting. To obtain a representation of xk that incorporates hierarchical context, we diffuse it
across G via the graph heat kernel Hτ = e−τL
. The heat kernel attenuates each spectral component
by e−τλi
, acting as a low-pass filter whose cutoff is controlled by a continuous scalar parameter, the
diffusion time τ. This continuous parameterization is essential: unlike discrete-step operators such as
polynomial graph filters, it allows the resolution of the hierarchy to be controlled by a single scalar.

We introduced TrajLift, a spectral framework that models verbal recall as timed trajectories on a
semantic hierarchy. TrajLift lifts each recalled word onto the hierarchy by heat diffusion and lets the
latency after each word modulate the diffusion time, so that structure and timing are encoded by a
single operator.

octen.snippet:
TrajLift: Lifting Memory Recall Trajectories with Latency-Modulated Heat Diffusion
Abstract
Verbal memory retrieval carries rich diagnostic information for Alzheimer’s disease through the order, hesitation, and categorical organization of recalled words, yet computational modeling of this retrieval process remains largely unexplored. A key challenge is that timing and hierarchical structure are diagnostically entangled: the diagnostic meaning of retrieval timing depends on its hierarchical context. We propose TrajLift, a spectral framework that models verbal recall as timed trajectories on a hierarchical graph. Our central mechanism is latency-modulated heat diffusion on the semantic hierarchy, a unified operator that lifts each recalled word into a representation of both multi-scale hierarchical structure and continuous retrieval timing. Formal analysis shows that the resulting representation is first-order separable into structural and temporal components with spectral selectivity across hierarchical levels. On synthetic benchmarks requiring structure-time interaction, TrajLift stays near-perfect on deep hierarchies where all baselines fail. On real-world clinical data, we show that TrajLift outperforms diverse baselines by jointly modeling timing and semantic structure, with gains that grow as retrieval timing becomes more informative. Code is available at https://github.com/kjw11/TrajLift.

Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is a prevalent neurodegenerative disorder in which memory impairment is identified as one of the most reliable early markers [1]. Verbal memory tests, which assess memory encoding and retrieval of newly learned word lists, have therefore been widely used as a standard AD

Memories are stored, retained, and recollected through complex, coupled
processes operating on multiple timescales. To understand the computational
principles behind these intricate networks of interactions we construct a broad
class of synaptic models that efficiently harnesses biological complexity to
preserve numerous memories. The memory capacity scales almost linearly with the
number of synapses, which is a substantial improvement over the square root
scaling of previous models. This was achieved by combining multiple dynamical
processes that initially store memories in fast variables and then
progressively transfer them to slower variables. Importantly, the interactions

octen.title: Theta-mediated conceptual reinstatement in vmPFC precedes perceptual reinstatement in ventral visual cortex during memory recall | bioRxiv
octen.snippet:
Abstract
When recalling past episodes, different features of an experience, such as conceptual meaning and perceptual detail, are reconstructed and reinstated across distributed cortical regions. However, current models of human memory remain unclear how these feature-specific reinstatements unfold over time, and whether they interact hierarchically during memory retrieval. Using magnetoencephalography (MEG) and time-resolved encoding-retrieval cross-phase classification analysis, we compared the time course of conceptual and perceptual reinstatement during cued visual recall. Conceptual information decoding in the ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC) preceded perceptual information decoding in the ventral visual cortex (VVC), and the two were expressed in distinct frequency bands: theta (4–8 Hz) for conceptual and gamma (30–40 Hz) for perceptual information. Cross-correlation and spectral Granger causality analyses revealed that during reinstatement conceptual information in vmPFC predicted and directed perceptual information in VVC, with theta-band information flow predominantly from vmPFC to VVC. In addition, bottom-up connectivity from VVC to vmPFC was expressed in the alpha band. These findings suggest that memory retrieval proceeds from abstract conceptual reconstruction to the reinstatement of perceptual details, mediated by theta oscillatory communication between prefrontal and sensory areas. We propose a hierarchical interactive model in which vmPFC initiates conceptual activation through theta-band top-down signals, while VVC provides alpha-band feedback for evaluating reconstructed perceptual details.

# Spectral Signatures of Memorization Basins in Diffusion Trajectories

arXiv:2611.01775
Authors: Achref Jaziri, Martin Mundt, Ahmed Imtiaz Humayun, Visvanthan Ramesh
Submitted: 2026-11-01
Subjects: cs.LG
Comments: 44 pages, 15 Figures

Abstract

Diffusion models are known to reproduce individual examples from their training data as a form of memorization with implications for generalization, privacy, and downstream use. Recent work demonstrated that memorized training samples reside inside contiguous regions of the data/latent space known as basins of memorization -- once a denoising trajectory enters a basin, under finite perturbations it irreversibly reproduces a memorized example. Prior empirical work on such basins in trained models has primarily focused on classifier-free guidance based detection and mitigation strategies in text-to-image models, leaving basin entry and their formation largely uncharacterized. In this paper, we present a geometric characterization of memorization basins for conditional, unconditional, and rectified-flow-based diffusion models. We observe a characteristic signature in the local spectrum of the function geometry that distinguishes basin entry: the emergence of a dominant singular mode followed by a sharp spectral recovery. This signature appears at two timescales: along denoising trajectories during inference and over the course of training. We further investigate whether these geometric signatures can be used to intervene on memorization. During training, we suppress memorization by acting on the dominant mode. At inference, we develop methods to identify trajectories entering memorization basins and steer them away. We find that these interventions remain effective even with low-dimensional approximations of the underlying geometry, and demonstrate that geometry-informed steering extends to large-scale text-to-image diffusion models.

# Memory as Reconstruction: A Distributed Transform-Domain Framework for Understanding Recall Dynamics

DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.20029032
Authors: West Jonathan
Published: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research), 2026-05-04
Type: article
Topics: Memory Processes and Influences; memory reconstruction; tip-of-the-tongue states; nerve injury; attractor model; large language models; constraint satisfaction
Cited by: 0

Abstract

This paper proposes the Distributed-Like Memory Hypothesis (DLMH), a framework in which memory identity is defined by reconstruction trajectories rather than stored states. Drawing on principles from distributed transform-domain representations (DTDR), it reframes recall as similarity-guided constraint satisfaction unfolding over time. The framework naturally accounts for recognition-recall dissociations, tip-of-the-tongue states, structured confabulation, graceful degradation under neural damage, and the phenomenology of remembering as "coming together." Classical attractor models are subsumed as a limiting case. Supporting computational evidence from large language models is presented, alongside four testable empirical predictions distinguishing the trajectory-based account from state-centric alternatives.

octen.snippet:
Many organisms can remember locations they have previously visited during a
search. Visual search experiments have shown exploration is guided away from
these locations, reducing the overlap of the search path before finding a
hidden target. We develop and analyze a two-layer neural field model that
encodes positional information during a search task. A position-encoding layer
sustains a bump attractor corresponding to the searching agent's current
location, and search is modeled by velocity input that propagates the bump. A
memory layer sustains persistent activity bounded by a wave front, whose edges
expand in response to excitatory input from the position layer. Search can then
be biased in response to remembered locations, influencing velocity inputs to
the position layer. Asymptotic techniques are used to reduce the dynamics of
our model to a low-dimensional system of equations that track the bump position
and front boundary. Performance is compared for different target-finding tasks. q-bio.NC, nlin.PS Z. Kilpatrick, Daniel B. Poll

Most AI memory systems are glorified databases with a search index. SULCUS treats memories as thermodynamic objects — born hot, cooling with time, reheating on recall, diffusing through edges. Here's how and why.

March 2026 · Digital Forge Studios

---

## The Problem with Static Memory

Every AI agent framework that offers \"memory\" makes the same mistake: they treat memories as static records. You write a fact, it goes in a database, and when you search, you get whatever the embedding model thinks is closest. There's no notion of *relevance over time*, no concept of *importance*, no mechanism for *forgetting*.

This creates two problems that compound as usage grows:

- **Context bloat** — every memory is equally important, so the system either dumps everything into the context window (expensive) or does naive top-k retrieval (misses critical context).
- **Stale knowledge** — a preference set six months ago has the same weight as one set today. The agent can't distinguish between \"the user used to prefer dark mode\" and \"the user prefers dark mode.\"

## Why Your AI Agent Forgets Everything (And How Thermodynamic Memory Fixes It)

> Most memory systems aren't memory systems at all. They're buckets. Here's why that breaks in production — and what a physics-based approach changes.

*March 2026 · Digital Forge Studios*

---

There's a dirty secret in the AI agent ecosystem: most memory systems aren't memory systems at all. They're buckets. You put things in, you pull things out, and everything inside is treated with identical indifference — the conversation from this morning weighted the same as the context from six months ago. Recent. Stale. Critical. Noise. The bucket doesn't care.

This is why your AI agent keeps forgetting what matters, keeps surfacing irrelevant context, and keeps bloating your context window with garbage from last quarter. It's not a model problem. It's a memory architecture problem. And it's solvable — but not by adding more storage.

## The Flat Memory Problem

Every major memory framework ships the same basic abstraction: a store with timestamps and similarity search. Mem0, Zep, Letta — respected projects, genuinely useful as *storage layers*. But storage is not memory. Memory is storage plus **physics**.

In current implementations, here's what happens in practice:

1. An agent interaction fires. Some facts get extracted.
1. Those facts go into a vector store with a timestamp.
1. On the next retrieval, semantic similarity scores determine what surfaces.
1. Everything in the store is a candidate. Nothing is ranked by relevance *over time*.

# TrajLift: Lifting Memory Recall Trajectories with Latency-Modulated Heat Diffusion

Verbal memory retrieval carries rich diagnostic information for Alzheimer's disease through the order, hesitation, and categorical organization of recalled words, yet computational modeling of this retrieval process remains largely unexplored. A key challenge is that timing and hierarchical structure are diagnostically entangled: the diagnostic meaning of retrieval timing depends on its hierarchical context. We propose TrajLift, a spectral framework that models verbal recall as timed trajectories on a hierarchical graph. Our central mechanism is latency-modulated heat diffusion on the semantic hierarchy, a unified operator that lifts each recalled word into a representation of both multi-scale hierarchical structure and continuous retrieval timing. Formal analysis shows that the resulting representation is first-order separable into structural and temporal components with spectral selectivity across hierarchical levels. On synthetic benchmarks requiring structure-time interaction, TrajLift stays near-perfect on deep hierarchies where all baselines fail. On real-world clinical data, we show that TrajLift outperforms diverse baselines by jointly modeling timing and semantic structure, with gains that grow as retrieval timing becomes more informative.

In this work, we model verbal retrieval as a graph heat diffusion process on the semantic hierarchy,
where each recalled word is treated as a localized signal on the graph that spreads to its structural
neighborhood. Heat diffusion on hierarchically weighted graphs has the well-known property that the
diffusion time (i.e., a continuous scalar) controls the structural resolution of the resulting represen-
tation. We exploit this to lift each node visit to progressively coarser hierarchical scales, capturing
within-category and cross-domain structure. We further extend this framework to encode temporal
dynamics by letting the observed inter-item latency modulate the diffusion time within a bounded
range, so that latency alters the representation at each scale without changing which hierarchical level
that scale resolves. Formal analysis shows that under this formulation, the structural and temporal
signals are first-order separable, and that the temporal encoding is sensitive to the hierarchical level.
